files.lesson.md: --- order: 51 unit: claims10 node: AC9M10ST01 n2 uses: [AC9M8ST02 n1, AC9M9ST02 n1] assumes: [AC9M8ST02 n1, AC9M9ST02 n1] connection: fan-poll title: Who did they ask? summary: "A report's numbers only speak for the people it asked. Find who answered, how they were chosen and who is missing, and decide whether the sample fits the claim." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A football club's website poll gets 50 000 votes. Does that settle what the city thinks?" --- A football club runs a poll on its website: "Should our city build a bigger stadium?" Fifty thousand votes come in and 92% say yes, so the club announces that the city backs it. The council has a city of 200,000 people to answer to, so it also phones 400 residents picked at random from the electoral roll. Which tells you more about the whole city? Have a guess, and we'll come back to it at the end. (The poll and the numbers are made up for the task.) ## Predict: big or random ```step stage: predict insight: "Choosing between a huge poll and a small random one shows who thinks a bigger sample is a better sample, and who asks who is in it." check: type: predict q: "The club's poll has 50 000 votes from people who chose to vote on the club's site. The council's survey has 400 residents picked at random. Which tells you more about what the whole city thinks?" options: - "The 50 000 votes, because more people is more reliable" - "The 400 picked at random" - "They tell you the same" actual: "The 400 picked at random. The 50 000 are mostly fans who chose themselves, and more votes from the same kind of people doesn't fix who is missing." ``` ## Run: how much of the city voted ```step stage: run insight: "Even a poll that reaches a quarter of the city can only speak for the people who answered, so the share of the population is not the question." check: type: number q: "The poll got 50 000 votes and the city has 200 000 people. What percentage of the city voted?" answer: 25 tolerance: 0 explain: "50 000 ÷ 200 000 = 0.25, so a quarter of the city. It's a big share, but the quarter chose themselves, and they're fans." ``` ## Investigate: source, size, how chosen, who's missing ```step stage: investigate insight: "To judge a report, ask who answered, how many, how they were chosen and who is missing. A big sample that chose itself can be worse than a small random one." tasks: - check: type: question q: "A shopping centre asks 300 people leaving its café whether the town needs more cafés, and 81% say yes. What is the biggest problem with the claim 'the town wants more cafés'?" options: - "The people asked were café customers picked for being easy to reach, so people who don't use cafés are missing" - "300 is a small number, so the claim is always wrong" - "81% is too high to be true" - "The centre asked people outside" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "A small random sample can still be fair. The trouble is who was asked." - "A high percentage isn't a fault in itself. Look at who the 81% are." - "Where they stood isn't the fault. It's who was standing there." explain: "The sample was chosen for being convenient and it is full of café-goers. It can say what café customers think, but not what the town thinks." - check: type: question q: "How were the club poll's voters chosen?" options: - "They chose themselves: it was a voluntary poll on the club's site" - "A random draw from the electoral roll" - "Every tenth person in the city" - "One person from each suburb" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "That's how the council chose its 400." - "That would be a systematic sample." - "That would be a stratified sample." explain: "A voluntary poll lets the people who care most answer. They can be very different from everyone else." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#lee" text: "Lee reads the club's poll. Click the line where the reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: big-sample-no-bias explain: "Line 3: a big sample is only reliable if it is a fair slice of the population. These 50 000 chose themselves on the club's site, so more of them doesn't make them more like the city." - check: type: question q: "A headline says 'teenagers spend 6 hours a day on screens'. The survey was a pop-up on a gaming website, and 1 200 players clicked and answered. Who does the 6 hours describe?" options: - "Gamers who visited that site and chose to answer" - "All teenagers" - "Everyone with a phone" - "Teenagers who never use screens" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "The sample wasn't drawn from all teenagers, so the result can't be stated for them." - "The survey didn't ask everyone with a phone." - "They aren't part of a gaming site's audience." explain: "The result describes the people who were asked. To say it of all teenagers you'd need a sample drawn fairly from all teenagers." - check: type: question q: "A school emails a survey to all 1 800 students and 140 answer. What might be wrong with using the 140 to speak for the school?" options: - "The 140 who bothered to answer might differ from the 1 660 who didn't" - "The school emailed everyone, which is always biased" - "140 is too many to be reliable" - "Emails can't carry surveys" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "Asking everyone is fair. The trouble is who replied." - "A sample isn't spoiled for being large." - "Surveys by email are common." explain: "When most people don't answer, the ones who do may feel more strongly than the rest. This is non-response." ``` ### Judging a report ```worked \text{Who answered?} :: People leaving a café who were asked at the door. \text{How many?} :: 300 people. \text{How were they chosen?} :: By being easy to reach, not at random. \text{Who is missing?} :: Everyone who doesn't use the café. \text{Verdict} :: It fits café customers, not the whole town. ``` Now try one yourself: a shopping centre asks 300 people leaving its café whether the town needs more cafés, and 81% say yes. Say what the biggest problem is. ### How were they chosen ### Find the mistake Read Lee's reasoning about the club's poll. Where does it go wrong? ### Who does it describe ### Who didn't answer ## Modify: would that fix it? ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing the poll's size or where it is posted shows what fixes a sample and what doesn't." tasks: - check: type: question q: "The club also posts its poll on the council's website, and 80 000 people vote. Is it a fair picture of the city now?" options: - "No: people still chose themselves to vote, and the fans are likely still the keenest" - "Yes: more votes always make a poll fair" - "Yes: the council's site makes it official" - "No, because 80 000 is too many" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "More of the same kind of voter doesn't fix who is missing." - "Where it is posted doesn't change who chose to vote." - "A large number isn't a fault. Who chose to vote is." explain: "More places to vote still leaves it voluntary. What makes a sample fair is how people are picked, not how many." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: the council randomly picks only 30 residents. Is that sample biased, reliable, both or neither?" options: - "Not biased, but not very reliable, because 30 is small and a different 30 could give a different answer" - "Biased, because it is small" - "Perfectly reliable, because it is random" - "Reliable, because it is small" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "Picking at random isn't biased. Being small makes it vary a lot." - "Random removes the bias but a small sample can still be far off." - "Small samples vary more, not less." explain: "Random picking is fair, but 30 people could easily give a different answer from the next 30. A bigger random sample would be more reliable." - hint: ["Sample size ÷ population, then × 100.", "400 ÷ 200 000."] check: type: number q: "The council picks 400 of the city's 200 000 people. What percentage of the city is that? (2 decimal places)" answer: 0.2 tolerance: 0.005 explain: "400 ÷ 200 000 = 0.002, so 0.2%. A well-chosen sample can be a tiny share of the population." smaller: check: type: number q: "What is 400 ÷ 200 000, as a decimal?" answer: 0.002 tolerance: 0.0001 explain: "400 ÷ 200 000 = 0.002. Multiply by 100 to make it a percentage." ``` ### Posting it in more places ### A small random sample ### A tiny share ## Practise: reading a random sample ```step stage: practise insight: "Turning a fair sample's counts into a percentage and an estimate for the whole population, and a review of percentages of an amount." tasks: - hint: ["Count in favour ÷ people asked, × 100.", "140 ÷ 250."] check: { type: number, q: "In a random sample of 250 students, 140 chose the pool for the end-of-year party. What percentage is that?", answer: 56, tolerance: 0.05, explain: "140 ÷ 250 = 0.56, so 56%." } - hint: ["Use the percentage on the whole school.", "56% of 1 500."] check: { type: number, q: "Use that 56% to estimate how many of the school's 1 500 students would choose the pool.", answer: 840, tolerance: 0.5, explain: "0.56 × 1 500 = 840. It's an estimate: a different random sample could give a slightly different answer." } - hint: ["Percentage of an amount.", "0.75 × 4 000."] check: { type: number, q: "Review: a website poll gets 4 000 votes and 75% say yes. How many votes were yes?", answer: 3000, tolerance: 0, explain: "75% of 4 000 = 0.75 × 4 000 = 3 000. It's a count of those who voted, not of the city." } ``` ### Percent in favour ### Estimate for the school ### Review ## Make: the council's answer ```step stage: make insight: "Back to the stadium: work out what the random survey found and say which result the council should trust." tasks: - hint: ["Yes votes ÷ people asked, × 100.", "216 ÷ 400."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "In the council's random survey of 400 residents, 216 said yes to a bigger stadium. What percentage is that?" steps: - ["$216 \\div 400 = 0.54$", "yes answers as a fraction of everyone asked"] - ["$0.54 \\times 100 = 54$", "as a percentage"] answer: "54" answerLabel: "Percentage who said yes" tolerance: 0.05 feedback: - ["92", "That is the club's poll, from people who chose to vote."] - ["216", "That is the number who said yes. The question asks for a percentage of the 400."] criteria: - "I used the 400 people the council asked." - "I divided the yes answers by everyone asked." - "I could say why this survey is more trustworthy than the poll." explain: "216 ÷ 400 = 0.54, so 54% said yes. That's a long way from the club's 92%: the poll's voters are mostly fans." - check: type: question q: "The club says '92% of the city backs a bigger stadium.' Which reply is best supported?" options: - "The 92% comes from people who chose to vote on the club's site, so it speaks for them, not for the city" - "The club must be right because 50 000 is a lot" - "The council's survey is wrong because only 400 people were asked" - "Neither result means anything" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "A lot of self-chosen voters is still self-chosen." - "A small sample picked at random can be fair." - "The random survey is worth using, with the limits that come with 400 people." explain: "The poll tells you about its voters. The random survey is a fair slice of the city, so it says more about the city, even though it is much smaller." ``` ### The council's result Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### The best reply The poll, the survey and the city are made up for the task. **Also used in** - **News and politics.** A poll's headline is only as good as who it asked and how. - **Your own surveys.** A survey of your friends speaks for your friends. - **Next lesson.** Five numbers: a way to summarise a data set that a few extreme values can't distort. ```teacher summary: Students judge whether a report's sample fits its claim by asking who answered, how many, how they were chosen and who is missing, and see that a small random sample can beat a huge self-chosen one (AC9M10ST01, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 14 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 13 min goals: - I can say who a report's numbers describe. - I can explain why a very large sample can still be a poor one. - I can use a fair sample's percentage to estimate for a population. struggle: "Thinking a bigger sample is always a better one. Ask: more of whom? If the new people are chosen the same way, is anything fixed?" before: > Students need the Year 8 lessons on bias and sampling methods and the Year 9 lesson on how two methods give different answers. The one idea: judge a report by its sample, not its size. The questions are on the board: who answered, how many, how chosen, who is missing. The library entries (fan-poll, screen-time-claim) suggest a class check with a real poll or report; use a real one only after you have read it yourself, because a real report is a copyright text and not reproduced here. The poll, the council survey, the café, the school survey and the gaming-site headline are all made up for the task. Self-selection (a voluntary poll), convenience sampling (whoever is easy to reach) and non-response (most people don't answer) are named in the tasks, not as a list to memorise. running: - "Predict: show of hands before the check. Expect most hands for 50 000. Don't say anything until the Run." - "Run: ask whether a quarter of the city sounds like a lot. Then ask whether it matters who the quarter is." - "Investigate: the worked example is the checklist. Ask students to say it back using the café." - "Make: the percentage is worked on paper first." stuck: - see: A student says the club's poll must be right because so many voted. ask: If another 50 000 fans voted, would that tell you more about people who are not fans? fix: No. More of the same kind of voter doesn't reach the people who are missing. - see: A student says the random survey of 400 is too small to trust. ask: Is it biased, or just small? What does small cost you? fix: It varies more from sample to sample, but picking at random gives every resident the same chance, so it isn't biased. - see: A student says 54% and 92% can't both be right. ask: Who does each number describe? fix: 92% describes the poll's voters, and 54% describes the random sample of the city. Both can be true of their own groups. stretch: Design a way to find out what your year level thinks about a school issue that is fair and doable in a week. Who is missing from your plan? support: A table with four rows (who answered, how many, how chosen, who is missing) filled in together for the café survey. leads: > Continues AC9M10ST01 (node 2). Where it leads: five numbers and boxplots (next), then reading and comparing data sets. The ethical side of data (node 3) is left to a class discussion. exit: q: A radio show asks listeners to text in their view and 4 000 do. Can the result be stated for the whole country? Why or why not? a: "No: the listeners chose to text in, so the result describes people who listen to that show and care enough to answer." explain: > A report's numbers describe the people it asked. Check who answered, how many, how they were picked and who is missing. A very large poll that people choose to join can say less about everyone than a small sample picked at random. ```

# Lee's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: lee
The club's poll got 50 000 votes, and 92% of them said yes.
That is a very large sample.
A sample this big must be reliable.
So about 92% of the whole city wants the bigger stadium.
# endregion
